documents.text: Now, the instruction on Yoga begins.
Yoga is the cessation of the modifications and fluctuations of the mind-field.
Then the Seer (pure consciousness) rests established in its own true, essential nature.
At other times, the Seer identifies with the fluctuations and movements of the mind.
The calming of the mind is achieved through steadfast practice (abhyasa) and non-attachment (vairagya).
Practice (abhyasa) is the continuous, dedicated effort toward inner stillness and stability.
That practice becomes firmly grounded when cultivated for a long duration, without interruption, and with reverent devotion.
Dispassion (vairagya) is the mastery that arises when one loses craving for seen or heard sensory objects.
For others, this spiritual attainment is preceded by faith (shraddha), energy/vigor (virya), mindful memory (smriti), meditative absorption (samadhi), and intuitive wisdom (prajna).
Or spiritual realization is attained through total, loving surrender to the Supreme Divine (Ishvara).
The sacred sound representing the Divine is the sacred syllable Pranava (OM).
Its repetition (japa) must be practiced with deep contemplation and feeling for its profound spiritual meaning.
The mind becomes serenely tranquil by cultivating friendship toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, joy toward the virtuous, and neutral equanimity toward the unvirtuous.
Austerity/discipline (tapas), self-study of sacred texts (svadhyaya), and surrender to the Divine (Ishvara pranidhana) constitute Kriya Yoga.
The purpose of Kriya Yoga is to cultivate deep meditative absorption (samadhi) and attenuate the afflictions (kleshas).
The five root afflictions are ignorance (avidya), egoism (asmita), attachment (raga), aversion (dvesha), and clinging to bodily life/fear of death (abhinivesha).
By dedicated practice of the limbs of Yoga, impurities are destroyed and the radiant light of wisdom dawns, leading to discriminative discernment.

The eight limbs of Yoga are: ethical restraints (Yama), personal observances (Niyama), physical posture (Asana), breath regulation (Pranayama), sensory withdrawal (Pratyahara), concentration (Dharana), meditation (Dhyana), and absorption (Samadhi).
The Yamas (universal ethical vows) are non-violence (Ahimsa), truthfulness (Satya), non-stealing (Asteya), continence/moderation (Brahmacharya), and non-possessiveness (Aparigraha).
The Niyamas (personal disciplines) are purity (Shaucha), contentment (Santosha), self-discipline (Tapas), scriptural self-inquiry (Svadhyaya), and surrender to God (Ishvara Pranidhana).
Posture (asana) should be steady (sthira) and comfortable/joyful (sukha).
Once posture is mastered, regulation of the breath through cessation of inhalation and exhalation is Pranayama.
Pratyahara is the withdrawal of the senses from their external objects, mirroring the inward stillness of the mind.
Concentration (Dharana) is the binding of the mind-field to a single sacred locus or point of focus.
Meditation (Dhyana) is the continuous, unbroken flow of awareness toward that single object of focus.
Absorption (Samadhi) is when that same meditation shines forth as the object alone, as if devoid of individual egoic form.
The three practiced together upon one object (Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi) constitute Samyama.

documents.original: पुरुषार्थशून्यानां गुणानां प्रतिप्रसवः कैवल्यं स्वरूपप्रतिष्ठा वा चितिशक्तिरिति
documents.transliteration: Purushartha-shunyanam gunanam pratiprasavah kaivalyam svarupa-pratishtha va chiti-shaktir iti
documents.text: Liberation (Kaivalya) is attained when the Gunas, having fulfilled their purpose for the Purusha, dissolve back into their source; or it is the absolute abiding of Pure Consciousness in its own radiant reality.
